items.title: Companies Act 2006, section 174: Duty to exercise reasonable care, skill and diligence
items.quote: A director of a company must exercise reasonable care, skill and diligence.
items.why: The binding duty on every director of every company, whatever its size. The standard is that of a reasonably diligent person with the knowledge, skill and experience to be expected of someone in that role, and with the knowledge the director actually has. The section says nothing about AI or technology; it is the legal root of the argument that directors must understand what they oversee. The existing briefing wrongly attaches this standard to section 172.

items.title: Companies Act 2006, section 248: Minutes of directors' meetings
items.quote: Every company must cause minutes of all proceedings at meetings of its directors to be recorded.
items.why: Why 'minuted' is a legal matter and not only good practice. Minutes must be kept for at least ten years from the date of the meeting. The duty is to record proceedings; it does not prescribe how much of the reasoning is written down.

items.title: UK Corporate Governance Code 2024
items.locator: Introduction (Application; Reporting on the Code), p.4-5; Principle O and Provision 29, p.12-13
items.quote: The monitoring and review should cover all material controls, including financial, operational, reporting and compliance controls.
items.why: The governance code itself. Applies to companies listed in the commercial companies or closed-ended investment funds categories, on a comply or explain basis under the Listing Rules. Provision 29 asks the board to monitor the risk management and internal control framework, review it at least annually and declare on the effectiveness of material controls. The words 'artificial intelligence' and 'technology' do not appear anywhere in the Code.

items.title: Corporate Governance Code Guidance
items.locator: Paras 222-223 (Risk governance: delegation, responsibility and accountability); para 272 (Material controls); para 31 (board minutes); para 89 (committee terms of reference)
items.quote: The board retains ultimate responsibility for the risk management and internal control framework
items.why: Source of the brief's quotation. The only place the FRC links AI to board controls: para 272 says material controls 'could include, but are not limited to' controls over 'information and technology risks including cybersecurity, data protection and new technologies (e.g. artificial intelligence)', and that the board decides which controls are material. Para 223 says a delegated responsibility 'should be clearly written in the committee's terms of reference'. The guidance is non-prescriptive and is updated in place (last update shown 1 April 2026).

items.title: Annual Review of Corporate Governance Reporting
items.locator: p.44 (Artificial Intelligence); sample described on p.5
items.quote: This year, we found that figure rose to 86% of companies
items.why: Source of the figure. From a sample of 100 randomly selected companies following the Code. 'Around half' mentioned AI in 2023. The review adds that it is 'important for boards to have a clear view of the responsible development and use of AI within the company and the governance around it', that some boards were updated on AI strategy and policy, and that some companies set up AI committees. A count of mentions in annual reports, not a measure of oversight quality.

items.title: The Wates Corporate Governance Principles for Large Private Companies
items.locator: Principle Three (Director responsibilities), guidance on committees, p.16; scope and thresholds in the Introduction
items.quote: The terms of each committee should be set out including authorities delegated to it.
items.why: The comparator for large private companies, which are outside the listed-company Code. A board 'retains responsibility' for final decisions when it uses committees. Written for companies caught by the 2018 reporting regulations (more than 2,000 employees, or turnover above £200 million with a balance sheet above £2 billion), which must state which governance code, if any, they apply. Pre-dates current AI and does not mention it.

items.title: Supervisory Statement SS1/23: Model risk management principles for banks
items.publisher: Bank of England, Prudential Regulation Authority
items.locator: Principle 2.1 (Board of directors’ responsibilities), points (c)-(e), PDF p.14; scope at paras 1.2-1.3, PDF p.3
items.quote: The board should receive regular reports on the firms’ model risk profile against its model risk appetite.
items.why: The clearest UK statement of what metric-backed board reporting on models looks like: a board-set appetite, regular reports against it, and challenge to the outputs of the most material models. In scope only for UK banks, building societies and designated investment firms with internal model approval; in effect from 17 May 2024. It covers all models, of which AI models are a subset.

items.title: Cyber Governance Code of Practice
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.locator: Section A (Risk management), Action 2; Section E (Assurance and oversight), Action 1
items.quote: Agree senior ownership of cyber security risks and gain assurance that they are integrated into the organisation’s wider enterprise risk management and internal controls.
items.why: A government code written for boards on a neighbouring technology risk, and the model the FRC's guidance points boards to. Voluntary, designed for medium and large organisations. Shows what a board-level mandate for a technology risk is expected to contain: named ownership at executive and non-executive level and assurance. It is about cyber security, not AI.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Playbook for the UK Government
items.locator: Governance section: AI governance board or AI representation on an existing board
items.quote: You should manage governance of AI through an AI governance board or AI expert representation on an existing governance board.
items.why: What government asks of its own departments: either a dedicated AI governance board or AI expertise on an existing board, giving 'oversight, accountability and strategic guidance'. Guidance for the public sector, not binding on companies; useful as a public benchmark for a named forum.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0), NIST AI 100-1
items.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
items.quote: decisions about risks associated with AI system development and deployment
items.why: International comparator. GOVERN 2.3 states that executive leadership takes responsibility for decisions about AI risk. A voluntary United States framework with no legal force in the UK; widely used as a reference for what top-level ownership means.
